introLesson.title: Introduction to Hamlet

sections.authorBiography: William Shakespeare was baptized in Stratford-upon-Avon on 26 April 1564, the son of John Shakespeare, a glover and town official, and Mary Arden. He probably attended Stratford's grammar school, married Anne Hathaway in 1582, and had three children: Susanna and the twins Hamnet and Judith (Hamnet died aged eleven in 1596). By the early 1590s he was an actor and playwright in London; from 1594 he was a sharer in the Lord Chamberlain's Men, who built the Globe theatre in 1599 and became the King's Men when James VI of Scotland became James I of England in 1603. He wrote or co-wrote about 38 plays and the Sonnets, and died in Stratford on 23 April 1616. Seven years later his fellow actors John Heminges and Henry Condell published 36 of his plays in the First Folio (1623).
sections.historicalContext: Hamlet was probably written between about 1599 and 1601, after Julius Caesar, for the Lord Chamberlain's Men at the Globe; Richard Burbage played the prince. Its story goes back to the Danish chronicle of Saxo Grammaticus (the tale of Amleth, written around 1200), retold in French by François de Belleforest (1570). An earlier English Hamlet play, now lost and often called the "Ur-Hamlet," was on stage by 1589, when Thomas Nashe joked about it. Revenge tragedy was a popular genre, following Thomas Kyd's The Spanish Tragedy (c. 1587). The play draws on live questions of its time: Protestant doubts about purgatory and ghosts (Hamlet studies at Wittenberg, Luther's university), the duty and danger of revenge, and succession, since Elizabeth I was old and had no heir.

publicationAndReception.publication: Hamlet survives in three early texts: a short First Quarto (1603), a long Second Quarto (1604–05) and the First Folio (1623), which differ in many lines and in whole passages. Modern editions, including the reading text here, combine them. It is Shakespeare's longest play.
publicationAndReception.then: It was popular at once: the Cambridge scholar Gabriel Harvey wrote in the margin of a book that it pleased "the wiser sort," and the First Quarto's title page says it had been acted in London and at Cambridge and Oxford. After 1660 it remained one of the most performed tragedies; the Romantic writers Goethe and Coleridge made Hamlet's divided mind the centre of interpretation.
publicationAndReception.now: Hamlet is perhaps the most performed and written-about play in the world. Readings have been psychological (Freud and Ernest Jones's Oedipal theory), political, feminist (Ophelia's madness and silencing) and existential. Films include Laurence Olivier's (1948), Grigori Kozintsev's (1964) and Kenneth Branagh's (1996); Disney's The Lion King (1994) borrows its plot. Lines such as "To be, or not to be" and "Something is rotten in the state of Denmark" are part of everyday English.

sections.overview: Prince Hamlet returns to Denmark for his father's funeral and finds his uncle Claudius on the throne, married to his mother Gertrude. Guards on the castle walls have seen a ghost that looks like the dead king. What the ghost tells Hamlet, and what Hamlet does and fails to do about it, is the play.

why does Hamlet wait? Thought, conscience, doubt, or circumstance?

sections.whyItMatters: Hamlet is the great play about thinking: about how hard it is to know the truth, to act rightly when you are unsure, and to live with grief, anger and doubt. Its questions about revenge, mental health, family loyalty and political corruption remain urgent, and its language is the most quoted in English.

spoilerOverview.text: The Ghost says Claudius murdered him and demands revenge. Hamlet feigns madness, rejects Ophelia, and stages a play (The Mousetrap) that confirms Claudius's guilt. He spares Claudius at prayer, then kills Polonius, hidden behind a curtain, by mistake. Claudius sends Hamlet to England to be executed; Hamlet escapes, sending Rosencrantz and Guildenstern to their deaths. Ophelia goes mad and drowns. Laertes returns for revenge, and Claudius plots a rigged fencing match with a poisoned blade and poisoned wine. Gertrude drinks the poison; Laertes and Hamlet are both wounded with the poisoned blade; Hamlet kills Claudius and dies in Horatio's arms. Fortinbras of Norway takes the throne.

segments.phase: I do: the book in one passage
segments.activity: Model a close reading of one passage using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “Something is rotten in the state of Denmark” slowly and put it in my own words: After the Ghost appears and beckons Hamlet away, the guard Marcellus says that something is rotten in the state of Denmark. Next, craft. I notice the image of decay applied to a whole country, as if the kingdom were a body going bad. The strongest word is “rotten”: it suggests corruption spreading from inside, which fits a murder hidden at the top of the state. Then, effect. What does Marcellus's line suggest about Denmark at the start of the play? My answer: Marcellus senses that the Ghost means a moral sickness in Denmark's rulers; the image of rot runs through the play, as Claudius's secret crime poisons the court, the family and Hamlet's mind.

segments.script: What the book is about (no spoilers): Prince Hamlet returns to Denmark for his father's funeral and finds his uncle Claudius on the throne, married to his mother Gertrude. Guards on the castle walls have seen a ghost that looks like the dead king. What the ghost tells Hamlet, and what Hamlet does and fails to do about it, is the play. Themes to track: revenge and justice: the Ghost demands revenge; is it a duty, a crime or both? action and delay: why does Hamlet wait? Thought, conscience, doubt, or circumstance? appearance and reality: "seems" versus "is"; feigned madness, spying and plays within plays. death and mortality: from the Ghost to the gravediggers, what death means and what it makes of us. corruption and the state: "Something is rotten in the state of Denmark."

segments.activity: Exit ticket on the author and context (answer given).
segments.script: Shakespeare wrote Hamlet around 1600, near the end of Queen Elizabeth I's reign, when no one knew who would succeed her, and revenge tragedies were popular on the London stage. How might that context shape a play about a disputed throne and revenge? Answer: Accept answers such as: worry about succession made a stolen crown feel urgent; audiences knew the revenge-play formula and Shakespeare questions it; the play reflects anxiety about legitimate rule.

criticalVoices.quote: If the dramas of Shakespeare were to be characterised, each by the particular excellence which distinguishes it from the rest, we must allow to the tragedy of HAMLET the praise of variety.
criticalVoices.speaker: Samuel Johnson, critic and lexicographer
criticalVoices.source: Notes to Hamlet, The Plays of William Shakespeare (1765), in Preface to Shakespeare, together with selected notes on some of the plays, general note on Hamlet
criticalVoices.useNote: Bell-ringer: list the tones you expect from a revenge tragedy; return to the list after Act V.
criticalVoices.linkedObjective: Introduce the play's structure and its mix of tones.

criticalVoices.quote: Hamlet is a name: his speeches and sayings but the idle coinage of the poet's brain. What then, are they not real? They are as real as our own thoughts. Their reality is in the reader's mind. It is WE who are Hamlet. This play has a prophetic truth, which is above that of history.
criticalVoices.speaker: William Hazlitt, essayist and critic
criticalVoices.useNote: Discussion: is identifying with Hamlet a help or a trap for analysis?
criticalVoices.linkedObjective: Consider why readers identify with Hamlet.

criticalVoices.source: "Hamlet and His Problems," The Sacred Wood (1920), "Hamlet and His Problems"

strategies.label: Wait time
strategies.howTo: Pause at least 3 seconds after asking (5 to 10 for DOK 3 and 4 questions) before calling on anyone, and pause again after a student answers so others can add on. Call on students at random, not only volunteers.

strategies.label: Think-pair-share
strategies.howTo: One minute of silent thinking or jotting, two minutes with a partner, then pairs report. Use it for every DOK 3 and 4 question so all students rehearse an answer.

strategies.label: Follow-up probes
strategies.howTo: Answer a response with a probe instead of a verdict: ask for the line that proves it, ask "why?" or "how do you know?", or ask another student to agree, extend or challenge.

strategies.label: Student-generated questions
strategies.howTo: Students write their own questions at each level (a recall, a "why/how" and a "should/what if" question), trade them, and answer a classmate's. The teacher picks one or two for the whole class.

strategies.label: Turn and talk
strategies.howTo: A 60-second partner check for literal questions, so every student says the answer aloud before one is called on.

strategies.label: Cold call with support
strategies.howTo: Call on a student by name after the wait time; if they are stuck, offer a choice of two answers or let them "phone a friend" and come back to them.

strategies.label: Socratic circle
strategies.howTo: Inner circle discusses for 5 minutes while the outer circle tracks evidence and questions; then swap.

strategies.label: Four corners / take a stand
strategies.howTo: Students move to Agree / Somewhat agree / Somewhat disagree / Disagree and must cite a line to defend the position; anyone may move after hearing evidence.

literal.label: Literal / recall
literal.scaffold: Sentence starter: “In this scene, … because the text says …”
literal.extension: Note how this detail is set up or echoed elsewhere in Hamlet.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?

inferential.label: Inferential / analytical
inferential.scaffold: Sentence starter: “The text says …, which suggests … because …”
inferential.extension: Test your reading against one critical approach (formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist) and say what it adds.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?

evaluative.label: Evaluative / synthesis / creative
evaluative.scaffold: Sentence starter: “I (dis)agree that … because …; someone might object that …, but …”
evaluative.extension: Situate your judgment in a critical conversation about Hamlet: whose reading does yours support or challenge?
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

questioning.alignment: Questioning design (our description; see docs/questioning-alignment.md): every lesson offers questions at three cognitive levels with DOK tags, built-in wait time, follow-up probes after each answer, think-pair-share for higher-order items and a student-generated question routine, with a level-specific focus set for each of the eleven rigor levels. It is designed to support classroom observation frameworks such as the NIET Teaching Standards Rubric (Questioning indicator); it is not NIET material and is not endorsed by NIET.

segments.activity: Students write to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Project the day's bell-ringer question (each lesson of Hamlet has its own). Students write silently for 5 minutes, then pair-share for 3. Call on one volunteer and one non-volunteer, and connect their answers to revenge and justice.

segments.activity: The day's key words in context, with verified word histories.
segments.script: Introduce the day's words in the sentences where they appear in Hamlet. Read each sentence aloud, ask students to guess the meaning from context, then give the gloss and the word history. Students copy one word into their journal with their own sentence.

Give the 10-minute background talk from the day's lesson: what happens in this scene, the context a reader needs, and the literary elements to watch. Pause once to ask a check-for-understanding question.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud in the day's lesson.
segments.script: Read the anchor passage aloud twice. Model the three steps out loud: what the words say, what craft choice stands out and why, and what effect it has on the reader. The day's lesson gives the passage and a full written think-aloud.

segments.activity: Guided analysis of a second quotation; expected answers given.
segments.script: Display the second passage. Students annotate it in pairs using the same three steps; circulate, then take answers to the two guided questions and confirm them against the expected answers in the day's lesson.

segments.activity: Independent annotation and a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph (exemplar given).
segments.script: Students annotate the scene on their own (three marks with a margin note each) and write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph on the day's focus, then begin the writing prompt at their assigned rigor level.

segments.activity: Structured discussion from the 30 tiered questions, with facilitation notes.
segments.script: Run a 10-minute discussion from the day's anchor question and tiered questions. Start with literal checks, move to inference, and end with one evaluative question that ties the scene to revenge and justice.

segments.activity: Scene quiz in the app and an exit ticket (answer given).
segments.script: Students take the scene quiz in the app, then answer the one-sentence exit ticket with a short quotation. Collect the tickets to plan the next lesson.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Restate the day's takeaway in one sentence, ask two students to name the line that best proves it, and preview the next reading in Hamlet.

objectives: Students will cite at least 2 quotations, with locations, to support each written claim about what the text says explicitly and implicitly (scored on the writing-prompt rubric).
Students will trace one theme across at least 3 sections of the play in the final paper, earning at least 70 of 100 rubric points.
Students will explain how characters, setting and point of view interact in at least 3 exit tickets, each meeting the claim-evidence-reasoning criteria.
Students will determine the in-context meaning of taught vocabulary, scoring at least 80% on the vocabulary items of the scene quizzes.
Students will write an argument with a clear claim, reasons and relevant evidence, scoring at least 80% on the unit test's short-answer scoring guides.

scoringGuide.full: 4 points: all four criteria met.

scoringGuide.zero: 0: off-text, restates the claim, or blank.
criteria: Judgment: states how far the claim is persuasive (fully, partly, not), not just agreement (1 point).
Support: one accurate, located quotation that supports the claim, with explanation (1 point).
Complication: one accurate, located quotation that cuts against the claim (ideally the passage named in the key), explained (1 point).
Qualified conclusion: weighs the support against the complication and says how the claim must be limited (1 point).

items.prompt: Evaluate this claim about the scene: “Hamlet exposes Rosencrantz as a tool.” Is it fully persuasive? Argue with evidence, including a passage that complicates it.
items.expected: The claim is persuasive only in part. In support, “The body is with the king, but the king is not with the body” (Act IV, Scene II, Hamlet) bears it out: He calls him a sponge "that soaks up the king's countenance" and riddles "The body is with the king, but the king is not with the body.". But “Hide fox, and all after” (Act IV, Scene II, Hamlet) complicates it, because this detail (hamlet runs) gives the reader a second explanation to weigh against the claim's reading. So the claim holds only once it is qualified: it explains much of the scene, but it has to account for that passage too, which it does not do on its own.

Riddle. The words “The body is with the king, but the king is not with the body” (Act IV, Scene II, Hamlet) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself.
The graveyard

To tell his story: horatio's farewell. The words “Good night, sweet prince; / And flights of angels sing thee to thy rest” (Act V, Scene II, Horatio) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself.
Hamlet's new trust in providence.

First soliloquy. The words “O, that this too too solid flesh would melt” (Act I, Scene II, Hamlet) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops appearance and reality: "Seems, madam! nay it is; I know not 'seems.'".

Hamlet sees the Ghost. The words “Angels and ministers of grace defend us” (Act I, Scene IV, Hamlet) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops corruption and the state: Danish drinking gives the nation a bad reputation.

The Ghost demands "Revenge his foul and most unnatural murder," and Hamlet ends with "The time is out of joint: O cursed spite, / That ever I was born to set it right!". The words “Revenge his foul and most unnatural murder” (Act I, Scene V, Ghost) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops revenge and justice: Hamlet swears to remember.

Hamlet's reluctance. The words “The time is out of joint: O cursed spite, / That ever I was born to set it right” (Act I, Scene V, Hamlet) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops revenge and justice: Hamlet swears to remember.

The plan. The words “the play’s the thing / Wherein I’ll catch the conscience of the king” (Act II, Scene II, Hamlet) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops action and delay: Hamlet berates himself for inaction.
Act III, Scene I
Characterization
Appearance and reality

Claudius admits "my offence is rank," Hamlet hesitates ("Now might I do it pat, now he is praying"), but Claudius admits "My words fly up, my thoughts remain below.". The words “My words fly up, my thoughts remain below” (Act III, Scene III, King) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops revenge and justice: Hamlet wants damnation.
Act III, Scene III

Gertrude's shame. The words “O Hamlet, speak no more” (Act III, Scene IV, Queen) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops corruption and the state: Gertrude's guilt.

He stabs at "a rat? Dead, for a ducat, dead!" and dismisses Polonius as a "wretched, rash, intruding fool," before making Gertrude cry "O Hamlet, speak no more.". The words “Thou wretched, rash, intruding fool, farewell” (Act III, Scene IV, Hamlet) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops corruption and the state: Gertrude's guilt.
Diction / vocabulary
Claudius's plan. The words “Do it, England” (Act IV, Scene III, King) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops death and mortality: kings and beggars.

Resolve. The words “O, from this time forth, / My thoughts be bloody, or be nothing worth” (Act IV, Scene IV, Hamlet) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops action and delay: Hamlet resolves.

Claudius. The words “When sorrows come, they come not single spies, / But in battalions” (Act IV, Scene V, King) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops revenge and justice: Laertes acts at once.

A pirate "of very warlike appointment gave us chase," and the pirates "dealt with me like thieves of mercy," so Hamlet comes home not by plan but by accident, carrying "words" that "will make thee dumb.". The words “I have words to speak in thine ear will make thee dumb” (Act IV, Scene VI, Horatio) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops action and delay: chance, not planning, returns Hamlet to Denmark and to his revenge.

Holding Yorick's skull ("Alas, poor Yorick! I knew him, Horatio"), Hamlet traces "Imperious Caesar, dead and turn'd to clay," then at the grave insists "I loved Ophelia: forty thousand brothers / Could not... Make up my sum.". The words “Alas, poor Yorick! I knew him, Horatio” (Act V, Scene I, Hamlet) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops death and mortality: every body comes to dust, from jester to emperor.

Hamlet's claim at the grave. The words “I loved Ophelia: forty thousand brothers / Could not, with all their quantity of love, / Make up my sum” (Act V, Scene I, Hamlet) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops death and mortality: every body comes to dust, from jester to emperor.

Hamlet's last words. The words “The rest is silence” (Act V, Scene II, Hamlet) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops death and mortality: Hamlet dies asking Horatio to tell his story.

The court is full of courtiers, officers and spies. The words “Dramatis Personae” (Dramatis Personae) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops corruption and the state: the court is full of courtiers, officers and spies. He is "son to the late, and nephew to the present king," and Gertrude is "queen of Denmark, and mother to Hamlet," so loyalty to his father and to the court are already in conflict.

Mood: cold and unease. The words “tis bitter cold, / And I am sick at heart” (Act I, Scene I, Francisco) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops corruption and the state: Denmark prepares for war with Norway; something is wrong. The play begins "Who's there?" in the dark, a sentry says "I am sick at heart," and Horatio fears the Ghost "bodes some strange eruption to our state.".

Famous maxim (this edition prints "ownself"). The words “This above all: to thine ownself be true” (Act I, Scene III, Polonius) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops appearance and reality: Ophelia is told not to trust Hamlet's vows. Polonius delivers maxims such as "to thine ownself be true," then orders Ophelia away from Hamlet, and she answers only "I shall obey, my lord.".

Polonius's advice. The words “Neither a borrower nor a lender be” (Act I, Scene III, Polonius) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops appearance and reality: Ophelia is told not to trust Hamlet's vows. Polonius delivers maxims such as "to thine ownself be true," then orders Ophelia away from Hamlet, and she answers only "I shall obey, my lord.".

The Ghost's farewell. The words “Adieu, adieu! Hamlet, remember me” (Act I, Scene V, Ghost) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops revenge and justice: Hamlet swears to remember. The Ghost demands "Revenge his foul and most unnatural murder," and Hamlet ends with "The time is out of joint: O cursed spite, / That ever I was born to set it right!".

Hamlet swears to remember: the Ghost's command. The words “Act I, Scene V” (Act I, Scene V, Ghost) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops revenge and justice: Hamlet swears to remember. The Ghost demands "Revenge his foul and most unnatural murder," and Hamlet ends with "The time is out of joint: O cursed spite, / That ever I was born to set it right!".

Polonius's method. The words “By indirections find directions out” (Act II, Scene I, Polonius) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops appearance and reality: indirection. He tells Reynaldo to "By indirections find directions out," and after Ophelia's report decides "This is the very ecstasy of love.".

Hamlet kills Polonius. The words “How now! a rat? Dead, for a ducat, dead” (Act III, Scene IV, Hamlet) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops corruption and the state: Gertrude's guilt. He stabs at "a rat? Dead, for a ducat, dead!" and dismisses Polonius as a "wretched, rash, intruding fool," before making Gertrude cry "O Hamlet, speak no more.".

Gertrude's description. The words “Mad as the sea and wind, when both contend / Which is the mightier” (Act IV, Scene I, Queen) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops corruption and the state: Claudius worries about public opinion. Gertrude describes Hamlet "Mad as the sea and wind," and Claudius admits "My soul is full of discord and dismay.".

Rosencrantz as sponge. The words “Ay, sir, that soaks up the king’s countenance” (Act IV, Scene II, Hamlet) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops corruption and the state: the courtiers serve the king. He calls him a sponge "that soaks up the king's countenance" and riddles "The body is with the king, but the king is not with the body.".

Laertes. The words “To hell, allegiance! vows, to the blackest devil” (Act IV, Scene V, Laertes) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops revenge and justice: Laertes acts at once. He cries "To hell, allegiance!" while Claudius notes "sorrows come... in battalions" and Ophelia gives "rosemary, that's for remembrance.".

Chance, not planning, returns Hamlet to Denmark and to his revenge. The words “Act IV, Scene VI” (Act IV, Scene VI, Horatio) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops action and delay: chance, not planning, returns Hamlet to Denmark and to his revenge. A pirate "of very warlike appointment gave us chase," and the pirates "dealt with me like thieves of mercy," so Hamlet comes home not by plan but by accident, carrying "words" that "will make thee dumb.".

Laertes's answer when asked what he would do to Hamlet. The words “To cut his throat i’ the church” (Act IV, Scene VII, Laertes) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops revenge and justice: Laertes would "cut his throat i' the church"; Claudius says revenge "should have no bounds.". Asked what he would do, he would "cut his throat i' the church," and he volunteers "I'll anoint my sword" with poison, while news of Ophelia's death ("There is a willow grows aslant a brook") feeds his fury.

Laertes adds poison to the plan. The words “I will do’t: / And, for that purpose, I’ll anoint my sword” (Act IV, Scene VII, Laertes) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops revenge and justice: Laertes would "cut his throat i' the church"; Claudius says revenge "should have no bounds.". Asked what he would do, he would "cut his throat i' the church," and he volunteers "I'll anoint my sword" with poison, while news of Ophelia's death ("There is a willow grows aslant a brook") feeds his fury.

Death levels the mighty. The words “Imperious Caesar, dead and turn’d to clay” (Act V, Scene I, Hamlet) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops death and mortality: every body comes to dust, from jester to emperor. Holding Yorick's skull ("Alas, poor Yorick! I knew him, Horatio"), Hamlet traces "Imperious Caesar, dead and turn'd to clay," then at the grave insists "I loved Ophelia: forty thousand brothers / Could not... Make up my sum.".

Acceptance before the duel. The words “the readiness is all” (Act V, Scene II, Hamlet) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops death and mortality: Hamlet dies asking Horatio to tell his story. He tells Horatio "There's a divinity that shapes our ends," says "the readiness is all," kills Claudius only after the poison is revealed, and dies with "The rest is silence.".

middleSchool.label: Scaffolded support
middleSchool.text: Supported track: write a five-paragraph essay explaining what Hamlet teaches about revenge and justice. Use at least three quotations from passages your teacher selects from different parts of the book.

hsFreshman.label: HS Freshman
hsFreshman.text: Write a multi-paragraph essay explaining how William Shakespeare develops revenge and justice in Hamlet. Use evidence from the beginning, middle and end of the book.

hsSophomore.label: HS Sophomore
hsSophomore.text: Write an argumentative essay analyzing how William Shakespeare develops revenge and justice across Hamlet. Trace the idea through at least three scenes and address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.label: HS Junior
hsJunior.text: Write an analytical essay on how the structure of Hamlet (its order, turns and ending) shapes the meaning of revenge and justice. Discuss at least one place where the book leaves the question open.

hsSenior.label: HS Senior
hsSenior.text: Write a sustained argument comparing two interpretations of revenge and justice in Hamlet. Weigh the evidence for each and defend the stronger reading in a mature, well-organized essay.

ap.label: AP
ap.text: Write a literary argument: develop a defensible thesis about how William Shakespeare's choices in Hamlet (a recurring element, structure and narration) shape a complex understanding of revenge and justice, weigh at least one competing reading, and sustain commentary on well-chosen evidence. Do not merely summarize.

collegeFreshman.label: College Freshman
collegeFreshman.text: Write a researched essay (4–6 pages) that places Hamlet's treatment of revenge and justice in its historical context, using at least two scholarly sources.

collegeSophomore.label: College Sophomore
collegeSophomore.text: Write a contextual essay (6–8 pages) on revenge and justice in Hamlet that reads the play against its genre and period and engages two published critics. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeJunior.label: College Junior
collegeJunior.text: Write a theoretically informed essay (8–10 pages) on revenge and justice in Hamlet. Name your critical method, apply it closely, and acknowledge its limits. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeSenior.label: College Senior
collegeSenior.text: Write a research paper (12–15 pages) with an original argument about revenge and justice in Hamlet, engaging at least four scholarly sources in Chicago style. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

graduate.label: Graduate / PhD
graduate.text: Write a seminar paper (15–20 pages) that intervenes in the critical conversation on revenge and justice in Hamlet, engaging the relevant scholarship and textual history. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

prompts.text: Analyze how William Shakespeare develops revenge and justice across Hamlet. Trace the idea through at least three moments (beginning, middle and end) and argue what the ending finally suggests.
Choose one recurring symbol, image or motif in Hamlet and argue how its meaning changes over the play and why that change matters to action and delay.
Analyze a central character's choices in Hamlet. Argue whether the play judges that character, and how its structure or point of view shapes your answer.
Two readers disagree about whether Hamlet finally endorses or criticizes its society's view of appearance and reality. Weigh both readings and argue for one, answering the strongest objection.

evidence.sections: at least three sections, from the beginning, middle and end
evidence.citation: Quote the reading text exactly and cite the act, scene and line (MLA style).
evidence.outsideSources: HS Senior and above: one scholarly or historical source; College Sophomore and above: two, cited in MLA.

rubric.descriptor: A specific, arguable claim that answers the prompt and organizes the paper.
Well-chosen, accurately quoted and cited passages from across the work, meeting the evidence requirement.
Explains how language, structure and literary elements create meaning; goes beyond summary.
Logical progression, clear topic sentences and transitions; introduction and conclusion frame the argument.
Formal academic voice, present tense for literature, correct grammar and MLA format.

criticalVoices.quote: But what Hamlet wanted was not a private revenge, to be followed by his own imprisonment or execution; it was public justice.
criticalVoices.speaker: A. C. Bradley, Oxford Professor of Poetry
criticalVoices.source: Shakespearean Tragedy (1904), Lecture III, Lecture III, section on the "external difficulties" theory
criticalVoices.useNote: Careful attribution: Bradley is summarizing a view he goes on to reject (Hamlet's obstacles were external). Students who use it must say so, then decide: does V.ii give us private revenge or public justice?

criticalVoices.quote: And, in the third place, there is a trait about which doubt is impossible,--a sense in Hamlet that he is in the hands of Providence.
criticalVoices.speaker: A. C. Bradley, Oxford Professor of Poetry
criticalVoices.source: Shakespearean Tragedy (1904), Lecture IV, Lecture IV, on Hamlet after the voyage (Act V)
criticalVoices.useNote: Ending lens: is "There's a divinity that shapes our ends" (V.ii) faith or fatalism? Bradley goes on to call it the latter; students argue for or against.
